paras.en: The cast of the Alva Film production, co-produced by Fresh Prod and RTS Radio Télévision Suisse, features Sewit Abadi, Sabbel Ceesay, Rebecca Baillif, Claudia Grob and Selam Tesfu.
Baillif talked to THR about his filmmaking process and the urgency of A Job Well Done.
Can you explain your filmmaking process and how it has fictional and real-life elements a bit?

It’s a very specific way of working. It’s not only based on what I have experienced. It’s more based on what my characters not only have experienced, but, especially in this movie, also how they feel and the way they behave in real life. So the whole work with them is to help them just be themselves as much as they can during the shoot.

When we shoot the movie, I have a script. But the script and what’s inside every scene is always very flexible because, for me, the main idea is that they know better. They are the experts for those things because that’s what they actually do in their real life. They are social workers. They work with immigrants in their everyday life.
Do you have any examples of how actors may surprise you with their input?

There is a scene in the film about sexual mutilation, and in the script, we had the idea that [the social worker] would be very angry. That was our idea because it makes us very angry, us as white people from here.
But when we shot the scene, Sewit, our actress, told me, “No, I’m not going to be angry. I’m going to be very careful and very empathetic.” That’s an example of how I work.
I guess that also allows you to avoid the white savior lens that could come into play?

They are the experts, so I’m just going to listen to them. And coming from documentary, it’s just obvious to me that I’m not the, as you said, white savior explaining to the world what immigration is and what it is to work with immigrants. This system of directing, this concept I have developed through my films, for me is now just the way I work. I don’t think I would be able to work another way.
Was any scene in A Job Well Done particularly difficult to shoot for you or the cast?

I wanted my wife Rebecca to be in the film because she also works as a social worker. We did a scene where she’s telling her boss that she’s actually being racist in a way. This scene was very difficult for her because she wouldn’t scream, especially at an elderly person. With her African background, she respects older people a lot. So it was hard for her to do the scene, but she really did it with a lot of authenticity. It feels so real that we really enjoyed it.
The film feels really timely and addresses a topic that is causing much debate around the globe. Are there any political angles you were particularly interested in?

The idea was to talk about how we in the Western world see the “useful” and the “useless” migrants, especially in Geneva, where we have a lot of international organizations and global companies. They are big companies that come there and hire people. Those expats are the good migrants that we want, and it’s easy for them to get papers and work because we need them. And the others, we don’t need because they may not have the same background. So for me, it’s absolutely unfair.

But the focus was on the social workers, because I wanted to do something about immigration, but I didn’t want to have another movie focusing on an immigrant. Through real social workers, we can see the impact that immigration has on us who have to deal with those laws that are very restrictive.

And, of course, I also wanted to talk about how if you don’t follow the rules, then you can become an outlaw yourself. There are many examples of how you cannot follow the rules. It’s impossible when you work with people every day, and they have needs, and you have to help them. It’s impossible to just follow the rules – that is what I wanted to say because that’s what they told me about their work.

articles.title: The Hottest New Tables in Hollywood During AFM
articles.author: Melinda Sheckells

paras.en: At the Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills, chef Edo Baldi gives the steakhouse an Italian accent, cooking beef and wagyu over an olive wood-fired grill. Don’t let the steaks distract from sweet corn tortellini with mascarpone and truffle butter, or the pancake soufflé for two. Terracotta tones and olive trees warm the restaurant. For casual meet-ups, Bar Baldi pairs thin-crust pizza with beverage director Jim Kearns’ limoncello-laced spritz.

Moving from Santa Monica into the former Lumière space, chef Jeremy Fox’s Birdie G’s brings its family-inspired cooking directly to Century City. Matzo ball soup, the Pickle Chick cutlet and rose petal pie join koji-aged steaks, handmade pastas and California vegetables. EDG’s design draws on midcentury supper clubs, with banquettes and expanded patio seating. The planned breakfast-through-dinner format covers the working day; martinis and Manhattans take care of happy hour and beyond.
267 N. Canon Drive, Suite A7, Beverly Hills

The former Palm steakhouse has a new cast of characters: a boar sculpture, greyhound statues and snake door handles. Quality Branded’s Bad Roman fills green velvet banquettes with diners sharing garlic babka and pepperoni cups with ranch. Chefs Craig Koketsu and Clint Ives oversee filet mignon topped with a cacio e pepe raviolo and lemon-shaped cheesecake. Order a pepperoncini martini or flaming Vesuvius Bowl. Shots arrive attached to miniature Italian cars.

Dinner can turn into karaoke at Little Luck, The h.wood Group’s Japanese izakaya on the Sunset Strip. Two private dining rooms come equipped for singing, while roughly 4,000 records supply the soundtrack. Chef Erik Idos, an L.A. native whose Nobu years took him to Hong Kong, returns with sashimi, nigiri, skewers and charcoal-grilled meats and seafood for sharing. Dark woods, amber lighting and lantern-like fixtures make Kevin Lee’s cocktails look as incredible as they taste.

For a meeting that starts with “just one glass,” Wally’s Century Plaza offers more than 50 possibilities. The new concept directly in front of the Fairmont pairs wines by the glass with a full cocktail program and a California-French menu that also draws on Wally’s signatures.
10200 Constellation Blvd., Suite 225, Los Angeles

Follow the fire to KYU, the Miami-born restaurant making its California debut at Century Plaza Promenade on Nov. 9. Roasted cauliflower, Korean fried chicken, tuna crispy rice and wood-fired short rib anchor the menu, with new dishes developed for Los Angeles. An open kitchen sits at the center of the more than 6,000-square-foot space, while a curved facade faces the plaza’s fountain.

articles.title: The world's super-rich are piling into alternative investments. Here's why

paras.en: The world's wealthiest investors are increasingly looking beyond stocks and bonds, pouring money into hedge funds, private equity and infrastructure assets, as market volatility and fears about stubborn inflation spur diversification.
From Asian billionaires to global family offices, alternative investments are becoming a bigger part of portfolios once dominated by traditional assets, said industry watchers

JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in Asia-Pacific surged 40% over the past 12 months, according to Dan Watkins, the firm's regional chief executive officer, underscoring the growing appetite among high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients.
"So you really have this huge appetite for alternative exposure happening in that ultra-high-net-worth, high-net-worth category," Watkins said recently at a media summit in Singapore.

The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns that stocks and bonds may not provide the same protection against market downturns as they once did, experts said.
"We are seeing a sharp increase in planned asset allocation to alternatives among the family offices we speak to," said John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier.

Alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios, surpassing traditional assets for the first time, according to BNY Wealth. Traditional assets accounted for 41% of allocations, the report found.

Wealthy investors are seeking diversification, income and access to investments outside listed markets, and concerns over elevated valuations, tight credit spreads and the growing correlation between stocks and bonds have accelerated the trend, Woods added.
Hedge funds are emerging as a favored option among wealthy investors seeking protection against market swings, particularly as traditional diversification strategies face growing challenges.

Olaolu Aganga, head of portfolio construction and analytics at Citi Wealth, said hedge funds have attracted the strongest recent interest among qualified clients, who are seeking returns less dependent on the direction of equity markets.

Private credit is another area drawing interest, offering investors contractual income streams, while some hedge fund strategies seek to profit from differences in performance between companies rather than relying on broad market rallies, said Woods.
Citi's 2026 survey of 351 family offices found that inflation was their biggest concern, followed by interest rates, financial system stability and market volatility.

Wealthy families are increasingly seeking investments that can generate income and help preserve purchasing power amid persistent inflation and interest-rate uncertainty, while diversifying portfolios against market volatility, according to Aganga.

The Citi survey, however, also showed public equities recorded the strongest net increase in allocations, suggesting wealthy investors are adding alternatives rather than abandoning traditional markets. "This is not a wholesale rotation away from public markets," Woods said.
Infrastructure has emerged as another major beneficiary of the shift, with the artificial intelligence boom creating enormous demand for data centers, electricity networks and digital connectivity.

Thomas Roland Guyot, head of private markets investment specialists for Southeast Asia at UBS Unified Global Alternatives, said investors are increasingly targeting assets that support AI, electrification and energy security.
Such investments potentially offer a combination of long-term growth and relatively predictable cash flows, particularly where revenues are supported by essential demand or long-term contracts.

Investor appetite is already showing up in fund flows. Net inflows into open-ended infrastructure funds rose 30% year on year in the 12 months through the first quarter of 2026, according to PitchBook data cited by UBS.

Private equity remains a cornerstone of wealthy investors' alternative portfolios, although they are becoming more selective. Family offices are increasingly favoring direct investments in companies, co-investments alongside private equity managers and purchases of existing fund stakes on the secondary market, rather than relying solely on traditional pooled funds, according to Citi Wealth's Aganga.
Such approaches can give investors greater control over their investments or opportunities to acquire assets at discounts, said Lombard Odier's Woods.

The broader shift is also being facilitated by the growth of evergreen and semi-liquid funds, which have lowered minimum investment thresholds and reduced some administrative hurdles associated with traditional private-market funds, Woods added.
Investing into alternative assets does not come without risks, even as mitigating those is driving flows.

Private investments can lock up capital for years, while valuations may be slow to reflect deteriorating market conditions. Even funds marketed as semi-liquid can restrict withdrawals when redemption requests surge.
"Improved access does not equal liquidity," JPMorgan's Watkins said.

Citi's Aganga also warned that performance can vary significantly between managers, while private assets may appear less volatile than they actually are because valuations are updated less frequently.

Investors must also guard against unintended concentration. A portfolio holding data centers through real estate, infrastructure and private equity funds may appear diversified while remaining heavily exposed to the same AI investment cycle, UBS' Guyot said.

For now, the flow of capital into alternative assets shows their increasing appeal among the rich, though not at the expense of traditional investment, with Woods pointing out that much of the new investment is being funded by fresh capital and excess cash rather than large-scale sales of stocks and bonds.

articles.title: Nvidia board meeting to decide CEO Jensen Huang’s fate stretches into evening

paras.en: Nvidia's board is meeting to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, CNBC confirmed late Wednesday, following reports of two extramarital affairs — one with an employee and another with an alleged Chinese spy.

Shares of Nvidia fell more than 9% in post-market trading after The Wall Street Journal first reported that the board was preparing to force out Huang. That news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Nvidia's vice president of health care.

The alleged relationship, according to the Times story, was with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell's bio on the Nvidia website says she's "responsible for the company's worldwide healthcare business, including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI, and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery, and healthcare analytics."
Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California in March, according to the Times.
Nvidia and Powell didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into the spying allegations.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message to Nvidia staff on Sunday. "I am deeply sorry."

Most of Huang's Nvidia shares are co-owned with his wife, Lori Huang, and are held in trusts. About 800 million shares are held by those trusts. Huang holds about 70 million shares on his own and has limited economic control over the company.

Rumors of an affair between Huang and Powell have circulated for years, in part because Powell lacks a background in health or science, according to a former employee who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter.

Healthcare is a smaller business at Nvidia. The company makes chips for medical devices and MRI machines, but they are a minor in comparison to the revenue generated from its advanced AI systems and graphics processing units, or GPUs. In recent appearances, including at the company's annual GTC conference, Powell has spoken about how Nvidia's AI technology can help accelerate drug discovery, assist providers and improve clinical efficiency. Powell has been leading the group since 2017.

Nvidia's stock was down 7% this week prior to the after-hours drop on Wednesday and is on pace for its sixth straight weekly slide, reflecting broad concern on the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The AI infrastructure trade was hit particularly hard last week after the midterm elections, as Democrats won sweeping majorities in both houses of Congress, and dozens of ballot measures past that could make building data centers more difficult.

Huang has become synonymous with the AI industry, and he is often referred to by his first name ,"Jensen," by customers and rivals. Nvidia has been one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom since its chips are used to train models and run large AI workloads.
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny and Kif Leswing contributed to this report

articles.title: Treasury yields edge higher as investors await fresh inflation and housing data

paras.en: U.S. Treasury yields edged higher Thursday as bond trading resumed after the Veterans Day closure and investors looked ahead to fresh inflation and housing data for clues about the economy and the Federal Reserve's next move.
The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was up 2 basis points at 5.0100%.

The 2-year Treasury note yield, which is more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was 5 basis points higher at 4.7800%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury note yield — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was steady at 5.3503%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The rise in yields comes as traders await more domestic data releases this week for fresh insights into the U.S. economic picture.
On Friday, the latest monthly producer price inflation print, which tracks wholesale inflation, is expected to show a 0.4% rise in October, down from the 1.3% surge in September.

Before that, investors are also looking out for October's home sales report from the National Association of Realtors, due later Thursday. Existing home sales rose by 1.5% in September to 3.99 million, up from a two-year low the previous month, and are expected to reach 4 million last month, according to Trading Economics estimates.

Oil prices were broadly flat in early trading, as Middle East negotiations remain deadlocked. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up less than 0.1% at $86.59 a barrel, while Brent crude rose 0.17% to $92.92.

articles.title: What an exceptionally powerful El Niño could mean for hurricanes, drought and flooding

paras.en: Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
You’ve probably heard by now, possibly even on this very podcast, that this year’s El Niño is on track to be one of the strongest ever recorded. But what does that mean for our weather forecasts?
Scientific American’s senior editor for Earth and environment Andrea Thompson is here to demystify this atmospheric phenomenon.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Thanks so much for coming on to chat with us.
Feltman: So we’ve talked, briefly, about this year’s El Niño in a couple other episodes. But let’s start with the basics just to refresh our listeners’ memories. What exactly is El Niño?

Thompson: Right. So it’s this, sort of, cyclical climate phenomenon. Its epicenter is in the tropical Pacific Ocean. And so basically in, sort of, normal times or on average, trade winds blow from east to west and across the tropical Pacific, and that, sort of, piles warm water up around Indonesia.

But in El Niño times, those winds weaken or can even reverse, and that means all of that warm water, sort of, sloshes back over toward the eastern tropical Pacific. And that can have really big impacts because that heat isn’t just limited to the ocean; it’s releasing out into the atmosphere. And that changes where clouds and storms form, which has, sort of, this domino effect in the atmosphere that can change major weather circulation patterns.

And, for example, it tends to quash hurricane activity in the Atlantic because you get a lot of what we call wind shear, so sort of cross-cutting winds, whereas in the Pacific Ocean, it tends to ramp up hurricane activity, which we’ve seen both of those play out over this hurricane season with really not a lot happening in the Atlantic and then whole bunch of flurry of storms in the Pacific.

And this particular El Niño is really, really strong; so the, the warm waters in the Eastern Pacific right now are just record-breakingly hot in terms of basically any El Niño we’ve seen in our lifetimes.

Feltman: Well and we’ve heard a lot about how this year’s El Niño is so intense. So I guess, a few questions there that we can tackle one at a time. How intense is it? How do we know? And then: What kinds of impacts are we gonna see because of that? So let’s start with just, you know, what do we mean by saying this is such a powerful El Niño, and how does it compare to previous years?

Thompson: Right. So we mainly measure that based on the sea surface temperatures in a specific part of the Pacific Ocean. And we, sort of, monitor what those temperatures are doing. If they reach a certain threshold, that’s when we say, “We’re in an El Niño,” and then if they get, you know, really high, then you could say, “This is a very strong El Niño.”

And these have been breaking records since September. I talk to climate scientists who are, kind of, just aghast at how strong this one is. Right now, temperatures in the, sort of, core part of the Pacific where we monitor El Niño are about 3.5 degrees Celsius above normal. That is astounding. They could reach four degrees Celsius above normal, when this event, sort of, peaks, which typically happens in the November-December timeframe for El Niños. And those just, sort of, absolutely smash any heat records we have, at least with direct temperature measurements. Those go back to, into the 19th century, and the, sort of, the record we have was set by an El Niño in 1877.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: We can also estimate sea surface temperatures going further back than, you know, direct temperature measurements based on things like tree growth rings, coral growth rings, and those tree rings tell us how El Niño–related precipitation changes happened. And then coral growth rings are actually a little bit more direct. How the coral grows is related to sea surface temperatures. And so those we can build out an estimate going back to around the year 1100, and this would probably set records even going back that far. So this is a truly astounding event.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: Wow. And do we know why this is happening?

Thompson: It can be hard to say. So, you know, El Niño and especially really big El Niños are still relatively rare events, and so you don’t quite have enough data to really be able to piece out why they happen when they happen. Anytime data is rare, it’s very hard to find a trend. There is some new research that indicates that climate change may be pushing us more toward these really strong El Niños. That’s based also in coral records. So it could be that we’re seeing more of these in part because of climate change.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But some of it’s also probably just the chaos of the Earth’s system that, you know, sometimes you’re gonna get one, and sometimes you aren’t. And of course, there’s a baseline warming of the world’s oceans that’s feeding into this a little bit, but even, sort of, subtracting that from the ocean temperatures, this El Niño is still outstanding.

Feltman: Right. Well, and so segueing into the impacts we can expect, you know, even though we can’t necessarily pin this on climate change, the fact that climate change is happening and global temperatures are already warmer and weather is already weirder probably means that a really extreme El Niño is maybe more worrying than it would’ve been a couple decades ago. Would you say that that’s correct?

Thompson: Definitely can, because for an example, El Niño tends to bring drought conditions to the Amazon. And the Amazon is already in a weakened state, both in part because of a previous strong El Niño that caused drought and contributed to wildfires as well as climate change acting on that and exacerbating those droughts. And then other, of course, land-use change happening in parts of the Amazon. So you don’t just have the effects of this El Niño, you have all those other things playing in.

And then we have various what are called teleconnections in scientific parlance, where El Niño has certain effects in certain places. And generally these are more robust when you have a very strong El Niño just because you have more input into the system from the El Niño. So, you know, you have the effects on hurricanes in the Atlantic and the Pacific, where we’ve seen almost no hurricane activity in the Atlantic this year and a flurry of storms especially around Hawaii and the Pacific. You’ve also seen a major drought and wildfires in Indonesia. That is a hallmark of El Niños.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And generally, the closer places are to where El Niño is, sort of, happening, the stronger the impacts are, which makes sense. But they can reach really far afield too, so you know, there are teleconnections in Africa. You tend to have more rainfall and flooding in the Horn of Africa but less rainfall and drought in, sort of, South Africa. And it’s going to be particularly interesting to watch this winter.

So, you know, with the climate being warmer than it was in the past, you know, it’s unclear how much of the precipitation from these storms may fall as rain instead of snow when what you want in the West is snow because that snowpack is, sort of, what gives you the water that lasts you through spring, summer and fall.

These storms also bring a lot of coastal waves, we already have exceptionally high sea levels off the coast of California right now ’cause it’s very warm there, too, and we have these, sort of, pulses of warm water that can come up from the main El Niño region called Kelvin waves, which I know we talked about before. And so all of that together could mean we have a lot of major coastal flooding in California this winter.
Feltman: Right. So how much do we know about how long the El Niño is gonna last?

Thompson: So we have a pretty good understanding of, sort of, the cadence of El Niño. It tends to always peak in the November/December/January timeframe. This one has ramped up a lot faster than ones we’ve seen in the past, so it got warm very quickly.

It’s a little unclear exactly how high it’s going to peak, and that might determine how long temperatures stay really elevated. If it peaks higher, it may take longer for them to come down. After it peaks, it’ll, sort of, slowly come down through the winter.

But winter is typically the time where we see the biggest impacts, at least in the Northern Hemisphere, in the U.S. It’s gonna last several more months. Eventually it will, sort of, exhaust itself, and ocean temperatures will get back to, sort of, more typical levels, and then we’ll be in what’s called, sort of, neutral conditions.

But the heat of an El Niño in the atmosphere always lags the heat in the ocean, the heat in the ocean peaks November/December-ish. Heat in the atmosphere follows a few months behind. So we’re going to see global temperatures stay elevated for longer. Right now it’s a little unclear if 2026 is going to be the hottest year on record. Very well could be. It’s definitely going to be up there, which is pretty remarkable because we started this year in, sort of, a weak La Niña state, so ...
Feltman: Which brings temperatures down?

Thompson: Down, yeah. So no one was expecting that this was going to be a contender. It will definitely be 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial this year, which would be the second year that’s ever happened after 2024.

[The year] 2027 [is] almost certainly going to be the warmest year on record because of that heat lag. And it will also be warmer than 1.5 C. And one thing I’ve talked to with some scientists is the question of: Do we come back down from that, or are we, sort of, at 1.5 C from now on? Now, that still wouldn’t technically breach the climate agreement ’cause that’s considered an average over many, many years, but it’s possible.

Now, if we swing over to La Niña, maybe we come back down below 1.5 C above preindustrial. It’s a little hard to tell. But, you know, this is definitely not going in the direction we want things to go in, for sure

Feltman: Yeah. I remember years ago, at this point, an expert I talked to said, you know, “We’re on an escalator. El Niño is us getting up on our tippy-toes, and La Niña is us ducking down, but the escalator keeps going up.” And that has really stuck with me all these years.

Thompson: Right. Yeah, and typically, sort of, El Niño’s temperature effects on the globe are temporary. Eventually that heat is radiated back to space. But what a couple climate scientists pointed out to me is that the same, sort of, feedbacks that happen with climate change, where you have sea ice melts or permafrost thawings that can, sort of, exacerbate it, those are sort of agnostic to where that additional heat comes from. So if you have more heat coming from El Niño, those might also ramp up those feedbacks and, sort of, effectively lock some of the El Niño heat into the system instead of it just being temporary.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: Well, not necessarily the most fun topic to discuss but always a pleasure to have you on. Thanks for talking us through this.
Thompson: Yeah, absolutely. Thanks for having me.

Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. If you’ve got any burning weather-related questions that you’d like Andrea to help us answer for you, send them on over to sciencequickly@sciam.com. We’ll be back on Friday to dig into some surprising new perspectives on the science of stuttering.
For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, this is Rachel Feltman. See you next time!

articles.title: Newfound invisible object in space could be a rare supermassive neutron star

paras.en: When it comes to neutron stars, size definitely isn’t everything, but mass can go a long way.
At least, that’s the case for a newly discovered neutron star candidate in a distant part of the Milky Way that has more mass than it should.

In a new paper published today in Science Advances, researchers at several Chinese universities and observatories and their colleagues describe their study of a binary system located thousands of light-years away from Earth in the Pisces constellation. In it, a red giant star is being orbited by what seems to be a very small, rather overweight neutron star.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Called J0008+0128, the system was picked up by analyzing data collected by China’s Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE), as well as the European Space Agency’s now retired Gaia space observatory.
The red giant appears clear as day in the data; what’s more interesting is what’s unseen—a hidden, hefty something that is gravitationally tugging on the red giant, making the star wobble to and fro.

After running through and summarily ruling out an exhaustive list of possibilities, the researchers concluded this invisible object is most likely a neutron star: the ultradense remnant of another massive star that exploded as a supernova, an event that compressed the dying star’s core into a city-sized ball of neutrons. Most neutron stars weigh in at about 1.4 solar masses, or 1.4 times the mass of our sun. This one, for reasons unknown, would be somewhere between 1.8 and 2.8 solar masses, with the best estimate pegging it at 2.2 solar masses.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The mystery is where that extra mass came from; solving it could help scientists better understand the complex astrophysical interactions that can create neutron stars—and the bizarre, extreme physics that occur inside them. One natural explanation for this plus-sized neutron star would be that it siphoned lots of material from its neighboring stellar companion—except that, in this system, the neutron star’s orbit around the red giant would be too wide.

“Because it’s so separated, that’s how they know that it has never dumped material onto the neutron star,” says Scott Ransom, a staff astronomer at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, who was not involved with the study.

That leaves two other broad possibilities: either neutron stars can be a lot bigger than previously suspected (“that would mean we don’t understand supernova physics very well,” Ransom says) or the supernova that led to this one’s formation was the result of two smaller white dwarf stars colliding and merging together. The latter scenario isn’t impossible, but such collisions should be very rare.

“It’s possible that there were two white dwarfs and the red giant, and the two white dwarves were in a really tight orbit, and they’re orbiting the red giant, and eventually those two white dwarfs collided with each other and turned into a massive neutron star,” Ransom says. Alternatively, he adds, what seems to be a single extraheavy object could, in fact, be a co-orbiting pair of run-of-the-mill neutron stars or a neutron star–white dwarf binary.

There is at least one other option. The unseen object is so dense that it could actually be a very low-mass black hole, Ransom says, a possibility he thinks is more likely because of the inferred circular shape of the object’s orbit.

“Astrophysically, there’s no reason why you can’t have black holes that small; it’s just that we don’t see any of them in our galaxy,” he says. “What [the orbit’s shape] probably means is that the birth of that neutron star or black hole was not especially violent.” The birth of a stellar-mass black hole is thought to be, in some respects, more sedate than that of a neutron star, with the latter imparting a heavier recoil that can “kick” the newly formed stellar remnant into a wild orbit—or off into deep space. “So the fact that the orbit is more circular might be evidence that this is a black hole and not a neutron star,” Ransom says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It may be impossible to ever truly know what this object is or how it formed. Follow-up observations with a powerful x-ray observatory to directly detect emissions from the mystery object could distinguish between the “black hole” and “neutron star” scenarios, Ransom says. But outside of that, the options are limited.

“There’s no radio pulsations that any telescope in the world will find in the next decades, probably, because they’ve already looked at it with the world’s best [radio] telescopes,” he says. “That's unfortunate because that would have been an ironclad signal that it was a neutron star. But besides that, I don’t know if there’s anything else they could do, so we may never know.”

articles.title: Metal-rich deep-sea ‘nodules’ also harbor diverse ocean life

paras.en: Small clumps of rock and metal in the deep ocean known as “polymetallic nodules” are teeming with life, according to new research—a discovery that could affect plans to extract these nodules from the seafloor.

The softball-size nodules, which take millions of years to form, are a potentially very valuable—and controversial—source of crucial metals such as manganese, copper, and more for deep-sea miners. These materials are a key component of electronics and could help meet the growing demand for technologies such as solar panels and batteries. But the practice has also raised concerns among researchers over the ecological impact of plucking nodules from the deep ocean.

Now, in a study published in the journal Scientific Reports on Wednesday, researchers add a new wrinkle to the controversial idea: in an analysis of hundreds of nodules collected from a particularly desirable mining area of the Pacific Ocean known as the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, they found thousands of microscopic animals living among the rock crevices.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

A single nodule, the researchers found, contained an average of 17 animals but could be home to hundreds of creatures, including roundworms, tiny crustaceans, and more. One species was particularly common: a single-celled protist the researchers have called “Thurammina sp. 1.”

The nodules, the study finds, provides a “distinct habitat” for critters that is different from the sediment around them. In fact, organisms collected 1,000 kilometers (about 621 miles) apart were more similar to each other than to communities in the sediment nearby, says study co-author Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo, a postdoctoral researcher at Sorbonne University in France. This suggests that the nodules themselves may be necessary for the survival of certain species, including Thurammina sp. 1.

The diversity of life hiding within the nodules should factor into plans to mine them, the study authors argue. Under President Donald Trump, for instance, the U.S. has sought to expand deep-sea mining to reduce reliance on foreign mineral imports. But there are few rules in place for how to do this responsibly, and countries differ on their views.

Japan, for example, is considering mining in its waters, whereas France has called for a ban on the practice. As Scientific American previously reported, other nations, such as Germany and Chile, have called for a pause, and the Pacific Island nations of Palau and Fiji have called for a moratorium. Meanwhile the firm Impossible Metals says it has tested an autonomous robot that can use artificial intelligence to retrieve nodules without disturbing nearby marine life.

“Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules,” said senior author Sabine Gollner, a researcher at the Royal Netherland Institute for Sea Research (NIOZ) and an honorary professor at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, in a statement. “This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.”

articles.title: A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut
articles.author: Meghan Rosen

paras.en: Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.
Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.
And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

articles.title: Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease
articles.author: Rachel Fairbank

paras.en: Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.
Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

paras.en: With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

articles.title: Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason
articles.author: Nikk Ogasa

paras.en: This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback?
Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.
But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

articles.title: Tattoos Affect Your Immune System in Ways Scientists Are Only Beginning to Understand
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: Humans have been tattooing themselves for thousands of years, for spiritual, cultural, or personal reasons.
Long before we were covering ourselves in ironic stick'n'pokes, butterfly tramp stamps, or full blackout tattoos, humans were marking their bodies with permanent ink.
But while history can tell us much about the culture of tattooing, we still don't know much about how the practice affects our health.
Introducing tattoo pigment into the skin triggers an immune response, and that ink obviously sticks around – though it doesn't always stay put.
Research shows that particles of tattoo ink can enter the lymphatic system and build up in the lymph nodes.

Lymph nodes are key hubs of our bodies' immune activity. Full of white blood cells, lymph fluid is filtered through them to clean out any debris it's collected on the way around your body. That includes misbehaving cells (i.e. cancer), bacteria, viruses, and foreign substances such as tattoo ink.

Rapper MGK recently found this out the hard way by rushing a massive blackwork piece that covers much of his torso, including the area of the lymph nodes around his armpits and shoulders. He says the process turned his surrounding skin yellow and made him "really sick."

Even without traveling through the body, tattoo pigment 'sets off' the immune system. Pigment enters cells in the dermis, the middle layer of skin, and is swiftly recognized as a foreign substance. The body sends its 'army' of immune cells, but the pigment particles are too large for these cells to remove.
That's what makes tattoos permanent, but it also sets up the body for a lifelong battle against an impossible-to-remove invader.
What helps make tattoos so permanent is that modern inks are made of a complex cocktail of chemicals.

"They contain pigments that give color, liquid carriers that help distribute the ink, preservatives to prevent microbial growth, and small amounts of impurities," medical microbiologist Manal Mohammed explained in an article for The Conversation in December 2025.
"Many pigments currently in use were originally developed for industrial applications such as car paint, plastics, and printer toner, rather than for injection into human skin."

Researchers have detected trace quantities of heavy metals in tattoo inks, including nickel, cobalt, chromium, and, on rare occasions, lead. Accumulated at high levels, heavy metals can be toxic, causing serious health problems such as internal organ damage, neurotoxicity, and increased cancer risk.
In some cases, these heavy metals triggered allergic reactions and immune sensitivity in the person receiving the tattoo.

We'll never forget the harrowing story of a Polish man whose immune response to a red ink tattoo included losing the ability to sweat, shedding all his body hair, and developing vitiligo, a skin-lightening condition.
"Colored inks, particularly red, yellow, and orange, are more frequently associated with allergic reactions and chronic inflammation," Mohammed explained.
"Red ink is particularly associated with persistent itching, swelling, and granulomas… small inflammatory nodules that form when the immune system attempts to isolate material it cannot remove."
The allergic reactions and chronic inflammation triggered by colored inks are partly due to the metal salts and azo pigments.
Azo pigments are organic compounds that are included in tattoo ink for their vibrant colors. They're used in textiles and plastics for that same reason.

But these pigments can break down into aromatic amines when exposed to certain forms of radiation: the kind your skin might cop if you spend too long in the sun, for instance, or if you decide the tattoo was a mistake and go in for laser removal.
And that's concerning, because lab studies have linked aromatic amines to cancer and genetic damage.

Tattoo pigments – especially black ones – can also include polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are found in soot, vehicle exhaust, and charred food. Many of these hydrocarbons are also classed as carcinogenic.
So far, there has been no strong evidence in humans that links tattoos to cancer – but lab and animal studies indicate there may be risks.
One observational study published late last year also found tattooed people had a 29 percent higher risk of melanoma (a kind of skin cancer), though other recent studies haven't found a link.
The immune responses that tattoos can trigger should also be taken into serious consideration before booking in for fresh ink.

"While current evidence does not suggest widespread danger, growing research highlights important unanswered questions about toxicity, immune effects and long-term health," Mohammed wrote in The Conversation.
"Chronic inflammation has been linked to tissue damage and increased disease risk. For people with autoimmune conditions or weakened immune systems, tattoos may pose additional concerns."
There's also the risk of infection involved in putting any foreign matter, including the tattoo needle, into your skin.

The tattooing process breaks the skin barrier, which is one of your body's important defenses against infections such as Staphylococcus aureus, hepatitis B and C, and, in rare atypical mycobacterial infections.
The tattoo industry is largely unregulated in many countries, so it pays to be aware of the risks and take things slow if you decide to get inked.
Related: Study Uncovers Hidden Ingredients in 83% of Tattoo Inks, Raising Concerns
It's important to talk to your tattoo artist about what inks they use and what hygiene practices they follow. And if you have any history of immune problems, talk to a doctor before going ahead.
"Tattoos remain a powerful form of self-expression, but they also represent lifelong chemical exposure," Mohammed concluded.
"As tattooing continues to rise worldwide, the case for better regulation, transparency, and sustained scientific investigation becomes increasingly difficult to ignore."

articles.title: Study Reveals What a Lifetime of Exposure to Fluoride in Drinking Water Does to Cognition
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: Fluoride does a world of good for your teeth, but its inclusion in drinking water is not without controversy.

While there's little doubt about its ability to help prevent tooth decay, public concerns about fluoride's potential harms have fueled opposition to water fluoridation for decades, with Utah and Florida becoming the first US states to ban water fluoridation last year.
Are those concerns justified? Not according to a new study in the Journal of Dental Research, at least with regard to fears that fluoride in drinking water might impact brain function.

Researchers in Ireland analyzed data from the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA), assessing the health of approximately 2,500 older adults in Ireland with an average age of 65, whose exposure to fluoridated drinking water could be traced across at least 50 years of their lives.

Depending on where they lived over the course of their lives, their exposure to fluoride differed due to varying levels of fluoride concentrations in local water supplies across Ireland, which introduced nationwide water fluoridation in 1964.

When the researchers sorted the participants into low-, medium-, and high-exposure groups – determined by residential locations – and compared them with results measured by two different cognitive assessments, there was no link between fluoride exposure and their cognitive performance.
In other words, several decades of exposure to fluoride in drinking water doesn't appear to be associated with poorer cognitive function in later life.

"Our findings provide reassurance that lifetime exposure to fluoridated drinking water at the levels used in Ireland is not associated with poorer cognitive function in older adults," says lead author and public health researcher Vinay Sharma from Trinity College Dublin.

"This is an important public health question, and we hope these findings contribute to an evidence-based conversation about the safety of the community water fluoridation program in Ireland and internationally."

A subset of the youngest participants had been exposed to fluoridated drinking water in the first five years of life, but that early-life exposure to fluoride also showed no association with cognitive performance.
The researchers point out that only 5 percent of their sample (124 individuals) had early-life exposure, however, which limits the strength of their conclusions on that aspect.

It's also worth noting that their finding of no link between fluoride and cognitive decline does not necessarily prove that fluoride is harmless to brain health – only that evidence of such harm can't be found.
The findings match up with a body of previous research that could similarly detect no link between fluoridated drinking water and cognitive function.

Not all studies agree, with two studies in China linking fluoride to cognitive impairment in elderly people, although the findings related to excessive fluoride exposure (fluorosis), and are not directly comparable.
Similarly, a meta-analysis in 2025 linked fluoride to lower IQ scores in children, although some of the evidence related to high concentrations exceeding those normally used in water fluoridation.
At normal levels, the new findings strengthen the case that fluoridated drinking water is safe for the brain.

"Fluoridation has been one of the most effective tools we have for reducing tooth decay at a population level," says dental researcher Michael Crowe from Trinity College Dublin, "so it matters that we now have long-term Irish evidence that it isn't costing anything in terms of cognitive health."
The findings are reported in the Journal of Dental Research.

articles.title: Study Shows a Single Nuclear Blast Could Disable 99% of Satellites in a Matter of Days
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: High above your head, it's getting a bit crowded.

In low-Earth orbit, more than 13,000 satellites are currently circling the planet. They're the backbone of your daily weather forecast, telephone and data communications, satellite internet services, and much more besides.
A new study warns that a single nuclear detonation at a high enough altitude could disable virtually every satellite in low-Earth orbit, knocking almost all of them out within a month.
If it sounds like science fiction, it isn't. Nukes in space have happened before.
During the Cold War, the US and USSR conducted 18 high-altitude nuclear explosions, ranging from Earth's upper atmosphere and up into space.
The biggest of these – called Starfish Prime – launched in 1962, detonating a 1.4-megaton nuclear warhead at an altitude of 400 kilometers (249 miles) above the Pacific Ocean.

The effects of the explosion ended up disabling several satellites at the time, and the US and Soviets agreed a year later to suspend all above-ground nuclear testing as part of the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.

The scary thing is, even a less powerful warhead than Starfish Prime could wreak unimaginable havoc if a low-Earth orbit detonation happened today, according to calculations by researchers at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (UW) and Princeton University.

In their study – which hasn't yet been peer-reviewed – the researchers simulated a 1-megaton nuclear explosion 500 kilometers above the South Atlantic, near a vast anomalous region where Earth's magnetic field is unusually weak.

The conditions there – in what's known as the South Atlantic Anomaly – would magnify the effects following the initial blast, trapping radioactive particles in pockets of space, through which satellites would keep traversing as they orbit Earth.
The same phenomenon unfolded after Starfish Prime.

"Electrons from radioactive fission-product decay became trapped in Earth's magnetic field, creating an artificial radiation belt that damaged satellites," the researchers, led by first author Zach Petersen, a UW astronomy-physics major student, explain in their paper.
"Unlike the prompt burst, a trapped belt repeatedly exposes spacecraft as they pass through it. A comparable event today would occur in a much more densely populated orbital environment."

In the researchers' simulation – incorporating the 13,300 satellites active in low-Earth orbit as of January this year – a nuclear blast in the region of the South Atlantic Anomaly would disable 25 percent of the entire fleet after one day.
At the end of day three, 78 percent of satellites would be disabled, which would increase to 98 percent after a week, and 99.4 percent by day 15.
Even in a scenario where spacecraft were given strengthened radiation protection, 99.3 percent of all satellites would be disabled within 30 days.
In another hypothetical situation, deploying a much weaker 100-kiloton warhead, neutralizing 99 percent of satellites would take a year.
But radiation wouldn't be the only peril.

As soon as a detonation occurs and the first satellites lose control over their maneuverability, it would increase the risk of collisions in space, with the researchers estimating approximately 20 resulting collisions within the first two years.
After 10 years, the collisions would have left approximately 3,900 new fragments of space junk orbiting Earth.

"Continued collisions among long-lived objects are expected to sustain debris production beyond the simulated decade, with the possibility of a slow buildup and eventual runaway growth on century timescales," the team writes, noting that sending new satellites up after the calamity would also be a gamble.

"Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft: new satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space."
Or, in simpler terms, as nuclear policy researcher James McKeon described the findings in a post online:
"Tl;dr: it would be bad. Very bad. Very, very bad. We must do everything we can to prevent this from ever happening."
The preprint paper is available on arXiv.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

paras.en: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

articles.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

paras.en: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
A massive new supercomputer simulation reveals how the first stars, galaxies, and black holes helped bring the universe out of its cosmic dark age.

- A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It follows 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how galaxies formed, how radiation spread through space, and how the universe gradually became transparent to light.

The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.
How the Universe Entered Its Cosmic Dark Age

The story begins with the Big Bang, when the universe existed in an extremely hot, dense state filled with electrons and other subatomic particles. This primordial plasma, described as initially smaller than a single atom, expanded rapidly and cooled as the universe grew.

Eventually, particles slowed enough for electrons to combine with atomic nuclei, producing electrically neutral hydrogen. Around 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe entered a period known as the cosmic "dark age."

Although the universe had become transparent to much of the radiation left over from the Big Bang, stars had not yet formed to illuminate the cosmos. Neutral hydrogen filled space and could absorb certain types of radiation, including the ultraviolet light that would later emerge from the first stars.
Lumina allows researchers to investigate how this early environment evolved, eventually giving rise to the galaxies, stars, and other structures that helped bring the dark age to an end.
How the First Stars and Black Holes Transformed the Universe

The simulation covers an immense region measuring 500 megaparsecs, equivalent to approximately 1.6 billion light-years. Within that volume, Lumina follows dark matter, gas, stars, and radiation (such as photons), capturing both the behavior of matter across enormous distances and the formation of individual galaxies.
One of its most important achievements is recreating two major changes in the early universe: hydrogen re-ionization and helium re-ionization.

Hydrogen re-ionization began as the first stars and galaxies produced increasing amounts of ultraviolet radiation. This energetic light removed electrons from neutral hydrogen atoms, a process called "re-ionizing" the gas. As more hydrogen became ionized, the universe became increasingly transparent to ultraviolet light, allowing radiation to travel across much greater distances.

This transformation helped clear the widespread neutral hydrogen that had dominated the early cosmos. Lumina reproduces the process in remarkable detail, showing how radiation from the first generations of stars gradually changed the conditions throughout space.
The simulation also follows helium re-ionization, which requires substantially more energetic radiation to strip electrons from helium.

The results point to different sources driving these two transformations. Early stars and galaxies appear to have been primarily responsible for ionizing hydrogen, while actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied the intense radiation needed to ionize helium.
This is the first simulation to capture both processes together, offering a more complete view of how the early universe changed.

"Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale reionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations," says study author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT.

The researchers are making Lumina available to other scientists, allowing its predictions about early cosmic structures to be compared with observations from existing and future telescopes. Such comparisons could help researchers better understand the events that shaped the first galaxies and stars.
Building a Virtual Universe With Half a Trillion Elements

Lumina gets its name from the Latin word meaning "lights." Its underlying technology builds on IllustrisTNG, an earlier simulation developed by scientists at MIT and other institutions, including members of the Lumina research team.
IllustrisTNG models how galaxies form and evolve by following the interactions of dark matter, gas, and other physical processes from the Big Bang to the present day.

To create Lumina, researchers upgraded the existing software so it could reproduce galaxy formation in comparable detail across a much larger region of space. They also incorporated a radiation transport model that calculates how light, including ultraviolet radiation, travels through the universe and interacts with surrounding matter.
Together, these improvements allow the simulation to track both the formation of galaxies and the enormous changes that radiation produces across cosmic distances.

The resulting model contains approximately half a trillion individual elements, including particles of dark matter and cells representing gas. It provides roughly 30 times the resolution of IllustrisTNG while covering a region 100 times larger in volume than previous leading simulations.

Recreating billions of years of interactions across so many elements requires extraordinary computing resources. The researchers used Frontier, one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, located at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

"At peak scale, the calculation brings together the equivalent of more than 100,000 CPU cores and around 15,000 GPUs," says Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, an MIT co-author of the study. "Making all of those processors communicate efficiently while continuously evolving trillions of interacting pieces of information is itself an extraordinary feat of computer engineering."
Watching the First Galaxies Emerge From Darkness
Lumina begins approximately 45 million years after the Big Bang, during an era when neutral hydrogen dominated the universe.

Researchers initialized the simulation using conditions based on scientists' understanding of that period. They then allowed the model to calculate how gas and dark matter interacted throughout its half a trillion elements as cosmic time progressed.
At the same time, Lumina tracked how radiation appeared, spread, and interacted with matter, including the ultraviolet light produced by emerging stars.

The result is a virtual universe that scientists can explore at dramatically different scales, from the arrangement of matter across enormous cosmic distances down to the development of a single galaxy.

On the project website, the researchers have released videos showing these processes in action. One offers a "zoom-in" from the entire simulated region to an individual disk-shaped galaxy. Another presents a time-lapse of the complete volume, showing how hydrogen re-ionization spreads across the universe over 2 billion years.

"On the one hand, it's evolving dark matter as well as the gas in the universe, and on the other, it's also tracking how radiation travels," Zier explains. "We see dark matter and gas start to clump in these over-densities. And when we zoom in, we can see gas is falling into these dark matter haloes. Zooming in more, we see this is where the first galaxies form. And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."
